# Endodontics, Pulp Space Anatomy and Access Cavity of Anterior Teeth

**Authors:** Pradip R. Chauhan, Joseph O. Daley, Girish Chauhan

**Source:** StatPearls - StatPearls Publishing

## Abstract

Anterior teeth—specifically the incisors and canines—play a central role in both dental esthetics and function. Beneath their hard tissues lies a complex pulp cavity, defined by a dentin-covered roof, a floor parallel to that roof, and canalicular extensions (root canals) projecting from the pulp chamber floor. The chamber itself is located within the crown, while the root canals extend apically within the root structure. These canals terminate in foramina, providing a vital conduit for blood vessels and sensory nerves. For the general dentist and endodontist, a precise understanding of this internal anatomy is indispensable, as the root canal system, integral to the central pulp cavity, is the primary site of intervention during root canal therapy. This system consists of a broader pulp chamber and a narrower pulp canal , both of which contain dental pulp, a specialized connective tissue that communicates with the periodontal ligament via the apical foramen. Access cavity preparation is more than a simple entry—it involves careful biomechanical shaping, removal of infected or necrotic pulp tissue, replacement of defective restorations, and elimination of unsupported tooth structure. In anterior teeth, practitioners may choose from several access strategies, including traditional (TradAC), conservative (ConsAC), ultraconservative (UltraAC), and truss (TrussAC) designs. As contemporary endodontics shifts toward minimally invasive approaches, these techniques warrant critical evaluation to balance structural preservation with effective canal debridement.
